newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria's first pluralist National Assembly opens.
newsitem.headline: Algeria's first pluralist National Assembly opens.

text.p: Fiery feminists and bearded Moslem fundamentalists rubbed shoulders with anti-Islamist hawks, former ministers and hardline left-wingers at Sunday's opening session of Algeria's first pluralist National Assembly.
"End of an era" wrote Algeria's Liberte newspaper on Sunday, describing in advance the gathering at Algeria's newly elected 380-seat National Assembly.

It includes 103 Moslem fundamentalists, 36 secularists, four Trotskyist activists, five centrists and 11 independents, alongside President Liamine Zeroual's 155 supporters in the National Democratic Rally (RND) and 64 members of the former sole ruling National Liberation Front (FLN). Twelve of the MPs are women.
The assembly session began at about 5 p.m. after a delay of nearly two hours caused by bargaining over the naming of the assembly speaker, party officials said.
The officials, speaking by telephone from Algiers, said RND leader Abdelkader Bensalah had failed so far to win a consensus among political groups to head the legislative body.
They said behind-the-scenes debate would continue between the 10 political parties represented in the assembly to forge an understanding on the naming of the speaker.
"Thirty-five long years of sole ruling party were the negation of the significance of parliament. It is no longer the case and it is a victory," said Liberte.
The newspaper said the session would usher in a new era of opposition activists who had suffered persecution for their ideals under the ruling party.
"The persecution over many years of women and men for their ideals matters little today. They will be present today in the Assembly. Today is a historic day," the paper said.

Among those entering the Zighout Youssef Palace, the seat of parliament on the Mediterranean seafront, are Rally for Culture and Democracy (RCD) leader Said Saadi and his rival Socialist Forces Front (FFS) interim chief Seddik Debaili.
Both were jailed and persecuted by the government in the 1980s for advocating human rights, multi-party democracy and Berber language recognition.

The colourful Louisa Hanoune, the only Algerian woman to lead an opposition party, takes her seat in the assembly. Her left-wing Workers' Party comrade Mohamed Benmustapha chaired the assembly's first session as the oldest deputy.

Radical Islamists used to call Hanoune "the only man" in Algeria for her fierce attacks on the government and constant demands to free outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) leaders to help forge a broad consensus to end bloodshed.
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which FIS had taken a huge lead.

The assembly met a day after Zeroual reappointed Ahmed Ouyahia as prime minister in a move analysts saw as underlining his eagerness to guarantee stability for the government to implement reforms under an agreement with the International Monetary Fund ending next April.

Ouyahia, an RND MP, has to form a government and forge an alliance with other parties to ensure support in the house. The FLN is seen as a natural partner of the RND but is setting conditions for joining any coalition.
The FFS and RCD have said they will not enter a coalition led by Ouyahia.

Analysts said the Islamist-oriented Movement of a Peaceful Society and Nahda parties were also unlikely to be associated in the government before local elections are held by the end of the year. The two Islamist parties won a total of 103 seats.
